title: Before You Give Up on Your Marriage, Read This… The One Thing Most Couples Forget That Changes Everything
paragraphs:
Before You Give Up on Your Marriage, Read This… The One Thing Most Couples Forget That Changes Everything
Every Marriage Needs Prayer—Not Because Every Marriage Is Falling Apart, But Because Every Marriage Is Being Fought Over
Nobody stands at the altar dreaming about divorce.
Nobody looks into the eyes of the person they love and whispers, "I can't wait until we become strangers."

Nobody imagines that one day silence will replace laughter, resentment will replace affection, and two people who once couldn't wait to be together will eventually feel like roommates sharing the same address.
Yet it happens every day.
Not because love always dies.
But because there is an enemy who hates what marriage represents.
Marriage has never simply been about two people.
From the very beginning, God designed marriage to reflect something infinitely greater.
The Hebrew Scriptures tell us,
"עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד"
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."
— Genesis 2:24
The phrase דָבַק (dāḇaq) means far more than simply "stay together."

It means to cling...
to hold fast...
to remain firmly attached...
to pursue covenant loyalty.
Marriage was never designed as a temporary contract.
It was created as a covenant.
That is why Satan attacks marriages relentlessly.
Because every healthy marriage quietly preaches the Gospel.
Every faithful husband reflects Christ's sacrificial love.
Every faithful wife reflects the Church's loving response.
The Apostle Paul writes,
"This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church."
— Ephesians 5:32 (ESV)
Marriage is theology lived out.
It is worship with ordinary people.
It is the Gospel wearing wedding rings.
That is exactly why prayer is not optional.
Prayer is the oxygen of a covenant.
Many couples spend hours discussing finances.
They schedule holidays.
They organise birthdays.
They plan careers.
They renovate homes.
They build businesses.
But they rarely kneel together.
Slowly, something invisible begins to happen.
Conversations become transactional.
Forgiveness becomes delayed.
Pride quietly grows.
Offence settles into the heart.
Little wounds become permanent scars.
The problem is rarely that God stopped blessing the marriage.
More often, the couple simply stopped inviting Him into it.
Jesus said,
"Apart from Me you can do nothing."
— John 15:5
Nothing.
Not "very little."
Not "less."
Nothing.
The Greek word χωρὶς (chōris) literally means "separated from."
A marriage separated from Christ may still survive.
But surviving is not the same as flourishing.
Without Christ, love becomes dependent on emotions.
With Christ, love becomes rooted in covenant.
Without Christ, forgiveness depends upon fairness.
With Christ, forgiveness flows from grace.
Without Christ, both spouses keep score.
With Christ, both remember the cross.
Perhaps the greatest misunderstanding about prayer is believing it exists primarily to change circumstances.
Scripture consistently shows something deeper.
Prayer first changes us.
Before God changes situations, He transforms hearts.
Many husbands pray,
"Lord, change my wife."
Many wives pray,
"Lord, change my husband."
God often answers,
"I'm beginning with you."
King David understood this.
After his devastating moral failure involving Bathsheba, he did not first ask God to repair his reputation.
Instead he cried,
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
"Create in me a clean heart, O God."
— Psalm 51:10
The Hebrew verb בָּרָא (bara') is remarkable.
It is the same verb used in Genesis when God created the universe from nothing.
David recognised something astonishing.
Only God could create a new heart.
Self-improvement could not.
Marriage counselling alone could not.
Time alone could not.
Only God could.
Many marriages do not merely need improved communication.
They need recreated hearts.
Prayer becomes the place where pride dies before conversations begin.
Imagine how many arguments would disappear if both husband and wife prayed sincerely before speaking.
Imagine how many wounds would heal if each spouse asked God to reveal their own blind spots before pointing out someone else's.
Prayer softens hearts that stubbornness hardens.
James writes,
"God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble."
— James 4:6
Notice the terrifying reality.
God is not neutral toward pride.
He opposes it.
Every marriage eventually faces two choices.
Fight each other.
Or fight together.
Only one strengthens the covenant.
Ecclesiastes reminds us,
"Though one may be overpowered, two can defend themselves. A cord of three strands is not quickly broken."
— Ecclesiastes 4:12
The third strand has always been God Himself.
Take Him away...
and the cord weakens.
Invite Him daily...
and what once seemed impossible begins becoming possible.
This does not mean every prayer instantly removes suffering.
Some of the strongest marriages have endured unemployment...
miscarriage...
betrayal...
cancer...
financial collapse...
or seasons of unbearable grief.
Prayer did not erase every storm.
It anchored them through it.
Jesus never promised His followers a storm-free life.
He promised His presence.
Before His crucifixion He declared,
"In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world."
— John 16:33

The Greek word τετέλεσται (tetelestai) spoken later upon the cross in John 19:30—"It is finished"—comes from the verb τελέω (teleō), meaning "to complete, accomplish, or bring to full completion." Christ fully accomplished the work of redemption. Because of His finished work, believers do not pray to earn God's favour; they pray from the secure position of His grace.
Prayer does not make God love us more.
Prayer positions us to receive what He has already graciously given through Christ.
Perhaps you are reading this with tears.
Maybe your marriage feels exhausted.
Maybe trust has been shattered.
Maybe loneliness has quietly settled inside your own home.
Maybe you've stopped believing anything can change.
If so, remember this:
The Bible is filled with stories of God rewriting what seemed beyond repair.
Abraham and Sarah laughed in unbelief, yet God fulfilled His promise.
Jacob the deceiver became Israel.
Rahab the prostitute entered the lineage of the Messiah.
David the adulterer found mercy through repentance.
Peter denied Christ three times, yet became a bold shepherd of the Church.
Saul the persecutor became Paul the apostle.
The cross itself looked like history's greatest scandal.
Yet through the resurrection, God transformed humanity's darkest moment into its greatest hope.
That is the Gospel.
God specialises in rewriting stories.
That is why our theme is not merely a slogan.
It is biblical truth.
Marriage is no exception.
Perhaps the miracle your marriage needs is not a dramatic event.
Perhaps it begins with two people kneeling beside the bed tonight.
No perfect words.
No polished prayers.
Just honest hearts before a gracious Saviour.

Even one spouse praying faithfully can become an instrument through which God works powerfully. Scripture encourages believers never to underestimate the Lord's ability to act through persistent, humble prayer (Luke 18:1–8; 1 Peter 3:1–2).
If this message stirred something in your heart, don't let it end here.
And if this message spoke to your heart, we'd love to hear from you.
Our community would be honoured to pray with you and for you.
Your support enables us to continue producing biblically faithful articles, devotionals, studies, and Gospel-centred resources that point people to Jesus Christ around the world.
Because one article can encourage a marriage.
One shared post can reach a family.
One faithful prayer can change generations.
And one surrendered life can glorify the Saviour who still restores what sin, suffering, and hopelessness have tried to destroy.
The greatest miracle is not finding the perfect spouse—it is discovering that Christ remains faithful even when we are not.
